title: Nammalvar's riddle
hookLine: a silent boy under a tamarind tree, and a riddle that wakes him
carry: the self lives in the body, but isn't it

lines: A LIGHT IN THE SOUTHERN SKY.
A YOUNG MAN WHO NEVER SPEAKS.
cards: A man is walking south, following a light. On pilgrimage in the north, the story says, he sees a glow in the southern sky.
He follows it a long way, to a temple town in the Tamil country, to a tamarind tree, and to a young man sitting in a hollow at its foot. Eyes closed. Not speaking.
People there say he's been that way since he was a baby. The traveler has one question for him, and it's a riddle.

teach.b: The young man is Nammalvar, the second name in our title. The traveler is Madhurakavi.
Tradition says Nammalvar was born and didn't cry, didn't nurse, didn't open his eyes, and his worried parents left him at the temple, where he sat under the tamarind, growing up in stillness.

teach.h: THE RIDDLE: WHAT WILL IT EAT?
teach.b: Madhurakavi asks him, roughly: if a small thing is born inside something dead, what will it eat, and where will it lie? And for the first time, the story says, Nammalvar answers.

teach.h: IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.
teach.b: It will eat that, and it will lie there. Two short lines, and Madhurakavi falls at his feet, his disciple for life. What did they mean?

One traditional reading: the small thing is the living self, the atman, born into a body that by itself is lifeless matter. Until it turns to God, it feeds on that body's pleasures and pains, and stays there.
That's one of Hinduism's oldest teachings in two lines: you are not your body.

teach.h: THE ATMAN: ALIVE INSIDE THE BODY.
teach.b: The body is where the self lives for now, and the self in it is alive in a way the body isn't. Other teachers take the riddle further, or differently; the tradition lets it stay a little open.

teach.h: THE SILENT ONE BEGINS TO SING.
teach.b: Then the silent one starts to sing. His songs, gathered as the Tiruvaymoli, are full of longing for Vishnu. In some, he speaks as a girl pining for her absent lover.
Sri Vaishnava tradition holds these songs so high it calls them the Tamil Veda. And Madhurakavi is remembered among the Alvars too, for a short poem in praise of no one but his teacher.

how: Sri Vaishnavas recite Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temple worship and at home, and the tamarind tree at his temple town is honored as the place where he sat.

o: Vishnu's Tamil poet-saints, Nammalvar among them
silent hermits who live under temple trees
pilgrims from the north who follow a light south

p: sat silent under a tamarind tree
followed a light from the north

s: Nammalvar was a well-known talker from childhood
tradition says he didn't cry or speak as a child; he sat silent under the tamarind.
his answer to the riddle was two short lines
it will eat that, and it will lie there.
the tradition gives one fixed meaning for the riddle
traditional readers explain it in more than one way.

games.q: you're Madhurakavi. you've followed a light a long way and found a young man sitting silent, eyes closed. what do you do?
o: leave; he clearly isn't going to talk.
ask him a riddle and wait.
shake him until he opens his eyes.
games.why: he asks a riddle about a small thing born inside something dead. Nammalvar answers, and Madhurakavi becomes his disciple.

practice: Rest your eyes low, like the young man under the tree, and sit still enough that your body gets quiet. Feel the breath moving in it. Then notice the one who is noticing the breath.
Many Hindu teachers say that watcher is nearer the self than the body is. If you pray, rest in God's presence in that quiet; if you don't, simply stay with the watching for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Nammalvar is the silent one under the tamarind, who answered a riddle and then sang the Tiruvaymoli.

orig.note: Tamil: a name for the poet-saint of the tamarind tree, said to mean our Alvar.

carryVoice: Your line: the self lives in the body, but isn't it. That's how one traditional reading hears Nammalvar's two short lines. See you tomorrow.
